clue.text: Plagiarism in writing Howard's End denounced

indicators.note: in tells us the word for plagiarism sits inside the word for writing

parts.note: prose is ordinary writing
a crib is something copied, plagiarism

indicators.note: Howard's End, the novel title, here asks for the last letter of Howard's

explanation.surface: A critic condemns copied passages found in an essay on Forster's novel Howards End.
explanation.walkthrough: The italicised title Howards End is a red herring: 'End' asks only for the final letter of Howard's, the D.
explanation.definitionFit: To proscribe is to condemn or forbid formally, so denounced is a fair synonym.

clue.text: European doesn't get a duck at the crease

indicators.note: doesn't get says one letter is left out of the word for the European

parts.note: a Pole is a European from Poland
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A European batsman avoids being out for nought while standing at the crease.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture (a duck is a score of zero; the crease is where the batsman stands) disguises a fold in fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleat is a fold pressed into cloth, a kind of crease.

clue.text: Small power group in Lagos could be newly rich

indicators.note: could be newly says the letters of the two words around it are freshly rearranged

explanation.surface: In Nigeria's city a little ruling clique might be nouveau riche.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be newly' sits between LAGOS and RICH and asks for their nine letters to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Oligarchs are the few who hold power in an oligarchy, a small ruling clique.

clue.text: Angry character alluding to a different place?

parts.note: cross means angry
a reference is a written testimonial to someone's character

explanation.surface: An irate person makes remarks about somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' means the testimonial an employer writes, not a person or a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cross-reference is a note directing the reader to another passage of a text.

clue.text: The air is uplifting in one mountain in Spain

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: in places the turned word inside the word for mountain

parts.note: ben is a Scottish word for a mountain peak

indicators.note: uplifting in a down clue means the word air is read bottom to top

explanation.surface: Breathing the bracing air on a Spanish peak is invigorating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uplifting' turns AIR into RIA, which goes inside BEN after I. BEN is used in Scottish mountain names like Ben Nevis.
explanation.definitionFit: Iberian describes the peninsula holding Spain and Portugal, so it means of or in Spain.

clue.text: Did new clothes do nothing for her either?

definitions.text: Did new clothes do nothing for her either?

parts.words: Did new clothes do nothing for her either?
parts.note: alludes to the tale of the emperor's new clothes, which clothed him in nothing, and asks after his female counterpart

explanation.surface: A question whether a new outfit failed to flatter a woman as well.
explanation.walkthrough: In Andersen's tale the emperor's invisible new clothes left him naked; 'either' asks about the woman of the same rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman ruling an empire, or an emperor's wife, holds the female form of the imperial title.

clue.text: Girl gets a pound a bottle

parts.note: Vi is a girl's name, short for Violet
L is the abbreviation for pound sterling

explanation.surface: A young woman pays a pound for a bottle.
explanation.definitionFit: A vial is a small glass container for liquids, a little bottle.

clue.text: Palaeolithic enigma involving Ancient Britons

indicators.note: involving signals the answer is wrapped up inside the run of words palaeolithic enigma

explanation.surface: The Old Stone Age poses a puzzle about Britain's early tribes.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the end of 'Palaeolithic' and the start of 'enigma'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iceni were a tribe of ancient Britain, led by Boudicca in revolt against Rome.

clue.text: No orders for amateur lecturer?

parts.note: lay means non-professional, amateur
a reader is a senior university lecturer

explanation.surface: Asks whether a part-time teacher has received no instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orders' means holy orders, ordination, not commands; a lay reader leads services without being ordained.
explanation.definitionFit: A lay reader is a church member licensed to take services but not ordained into holy orders.

clue.text: Sweet fruit with trifle

parts.note: the gooseberry is a fruit
to fool is to trifle or play about

explanation.surface: A dessert of fruit served with a trifle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trifle' looks like the pudding, but it is the verb meaning to mess about.
explanation.definitionFit: Gooseberry fool is a British pudding of stewed fruit folded into cream, a sweet course.

clue.text: Perfect example of English- Greek letter book

parts.note: pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
a tome is a large book

explanation.surface: A model case drawn from an English-Greek alphabet book.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitome is the typical embodiment of a quality, a perfect example.

clue.text: Issue expert information saying why

parts.note: a pro is a professional, an expert
gen is British slang for information

indicators.note: saying tells us to take the sound of the word why

parts.note: why spoken sounds like the letter Y

explanation.surface: An authority publishes information explaining the reasons behind something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a verb, but it is the noun meaning offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: Progeny are offspring, which in legal language are one's issue.

clue.text: Exhaust about to scrape — new inside needed to emit vapour

indicators.note: about here means going round, so the word for exhaust surrounds the rest

parts.note: to tire is to exhaust

indicators.note: inside places the letter for new within the word for scrape

parts.note: to rasp is to scrape

explanation.surface: A mechanic's note: the car's exhaust scrapes and needs new internals before it fumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside' puts N within RASP to make RANSP, and 'about' wraps TIRE round that. 'Exhaust' is a verb, not the car part.
explanation.definitionFit: To transpire, in its botanical sense, is for a plant to give off water vapour through its leaves.

clue.text: Mine in Kent possibly causes ill-will

indicators.note: in places the word for mine inside the region letters

parts.note: Kent is a county in the South East of England, abbreviated SE
a pit is a coal mine

explanation.surface: Trouble at a Kentish colliery causes bad feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent, the English county south-east of London, once had coal mines, so the surface is realistic.
explanation.definitionFit: Spite is malice, the wish to hurt someone, which is ill-will.

clue.text: Northern Ireland revolutionary finds suitable position

parts.note: Che Guevara was the Argentine-born revolutionary

explanation.surface: An Ulster rebel finds a fitting role for himself.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a role or place that exactly suits someone.

clue.text: Wear this to embrace the clergy

parts.note: to neck is to kiss and cuddle, embrace
the cloth is a collective term for the clergy

explanation.surface: A suggestion to dress in something to welcome the priesthood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embrace' is the slang verb neck, to cuddle, and 'the cloth' means the clergy collectively.
explanation.definitionFit: A neckcloth is a cravat, a garment worn around the neck.

clue.text: Noble seed's poorly with epistaxis

indicators.note: poorly suggests the words noble seed are in a bad way and broken up

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: An aristocrat's offspring is unwell with a medical condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poorly' rearranges NOBLESEED. Epistaxis is the medical term for the condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Epistaxis is the medical word for bleeding from the nose.

clue.text: Out-going type to vex rotter maybe

indicators.note: maybe suggests the words vex rotter could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A sociable person likes to annoy a cad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' asks for VEXROTTER to be rearranged. ROTTER is old British slang for a scoundrel.
explanation.definitionFit: An extrovert is an outgoing, sociable person.

clue.text: Small caskets placed in Indian classes

indicators.note: in puts the word for placed inside the word for Indian classes

parts.note: castes are the hereditary social classes of Hindu India
set means placed

explanation.surface: Little boxes are put in Indian schoolrooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'classes' looks like schoolrooms, but it means the social castes of India.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassette originally meant a small box or casket for valuables.

clue.text: He-otter, wild to boot

indicators.note: wild signals the letters of he-otter run riot into a new order

explanation.surface: A male otter roams free, untamed into the bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges HEOTTER. 'to boot' means in addition, not footwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Thereto is a formal word meaning in addition to that, besides.

clue.text: Chemist loses girl to poet

indicators.note: loses says the girl's name is taken out of the word for chemist

parts.note: a dispenser prepares medicines, a pharmacist or chemist
Di is a girl's name, short for Diana

explanation.surface: A pharmacist is jilted by a young woman in favour of a versifier.
explanation.definitionFit: Edmund Spenser was the Elizabethan poet who wrote The Faerie Queene.

clue.text: Spinner operating from either end

indicators.note: operating from either end says the word works the same read in both directions

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A rotating machine part runs from both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer reads the same forwards and backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotor is the rotating part of an engine or helicopter, something that spins.

clue.text: One of Lord Arthur Savile's?

parts.note: refers to the Oscar Wilde story about Lord Arthur Savile, whose title names his misdeed

explanation.surface: A question about something belonging to a Wildean aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar Wilde's short story is called Lord Arthur Savile's Crime; the clue asks for an example of what he committed.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of the Wilde story commits a murder, an offence against the law.

clue.text: The result of having children

parts.note: describes offspring, the outcome of becoming a parent, in old legal language

explanation.surface: What comes from becoming a parent.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both an outcome and, legally, a person's children, and the clue plays on both.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue is a formal word for offspring and also means outcome or result.

clue.text: Who said Gama was a disagreeable man?

definitions.text: Who said Gama was a disagreeable man?

parts.words: Who said Gama was a disagreeable man?
parts.note: King Gama in Gilbert and Sullivan's Princess Ida complains in his song that all people call him disagreeable

explanation.surface: A question about who slandered a man named Gama.
explanation.walkthrough: In Princess Ida King Gama sings that, for all his kindness, all and sundry say he is such a disagreeable man.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means all people, every person, which is who Gama says calls him disagreeable.

clue.text: Give in return

explanation.definitionFit: Yield means both to give way and the profit an investment returns.

clue.text: Small bone is close to disaster

indicators.note: to disaster suggests the letters of is close are wrecked and rearranged

explanation.surface: A tiny skeleton fragment is near to catastrophe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to disaster' rearranges ISCLOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: An ossicle is a small bone, especially one of the three in the middle ear.

clue.text: This language is nothing among bridge players

indicators.note: among places the word for nothing between the bridge player letters

parts.note: bridge players sit at compass points, abbreviated S, N and E
love means a score of nothing in tennis

explanation.surface: A tongue is said to be useless at a card table.
explanation.walkthrough: LOVE goes between S and NE. The four bridge players are North, South, East and West.
explanation.definitionFit: Slovene is the South Slavic language of Slovenia.

clue.text: Pay attention to what the man had said

indicators.note: said means the words for what the man had are to be heard aloud

parts.note: the man had contracts to he'd

explanation.surface: Listen carefully to what the fellow said.
explanation.walkthrough: HE'D (he had) sounds the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To heed is to take notice of, pay attention to.

clue.text: Commanding officer told about right to be associated

indicators.note: about places the word told around the letter for right

parts.note: related means told, narrated

explanation.surface: A senior officer reported on the correct way to be linked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps RELATED round R, giving RRELATED after CO.
explanation.definitionFit: Correlated means mutually linked or connected, so associated fits.
